hints: Focus on what makes any heart valve open or close, think about pressure on the two sides of the semilunar valves (ventricle vs artery).
Remember valves always prevent backflow, so ask yourself when blood would try to flow backwards from the arteries into the ventricles.
walkthrough:
**Recall How Valves Work**

Think of heart valves as one-way doors. They do not need muscles to open and close, they respond simply to pressure differences.

Rule to remember: blood always flows from high pressure to low pressure, and a valve closes to stop backflow.

**Apply This to the Semilunar Valves**

The semilunar valves sit between the ventricles and the large arteries (aorta and pulmonary artery).

When ventricles contract, ventricular pressure > arterial pressure, so valves open and blood is pushed out. When ventricles relax, ventricular pressure falls < arterial pressure, so blood tries to fall back and the valves snap shut.

**Check the Other Statements**

The septum separates left from right, not atria from ventricles. The pacemaker in the right atrium (SAN) starts the impulse, it does not delay it. And it is the atrioventricular valves, not vein valves, that stop backflow into the ventricles.

options.A: Correct. When ventricular pressure drops below arterial pressure during diastole, blood starts to flow back and closes the semilunar valves, producing the second heart sound.
options.B: False. The septum separates left and right sides of the heart to prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, not atria from ventricles.
options.C: False. The patch in the right atrium is the SAN which initiates the impulse, while delay happens at the AVN between the atria and ventricles.
options.D: False. Valves in veins prevent backflow in veins toward the tissues, while backflow into the ventricles is prevented by the atrioventricular valves.
